The final product presents the most detailed view scientists have ever had of wind-carved Martian cliffs, including crags known as yardangs.

"This scene has a wildness that reminds me of a road trip through Monument Valley, Arizona. You can almost feel the silence and the endless open space under the sky,” Ashwin Vasavada, a planetary scientist and the Curiosity project scientist, tells Reuters’ Will Dunham. “But as familiar as that sounds, the ⁠sky is ​orange and the sunrise has shades of blue. It's like Earth, but it's definitely ​Mars.”

blocks.x: The yardangs sit on the northwest side of a three-mile-tall mountain called Mount Sharp, and both features sit in Mars’ Gale Crater, according to the outlet. Curiosity landed on Mars in 2012 and has been climbing Mount Sharp since 2014. On August 26, it reached 0.6 miles of elevation, which is a record for Martian rovers.

Mount Sharp’s layers preserve materials from different periods of Mars’ history. Their analysis has shed light on the lakes and streams that existed there billions of years ago, when the Red Planet hosted a much wetter environment. When the water dried up it left behind layers of minerals, and when the deposits stopped accumulating on Mount Sharp, wind possibly eroded the yardangs into being.

However, “the yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” Vasavada says in a NASA statement. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.” In fact, the yardangs don’t seem to be part of the rest of Mount Sharp’s layers, Vasavada adds to Reuters.

Curiosity’s objective is to understand if Mars could have ever hosted extraterrestrial microbes, and the rover made headlines earlier this year when it discovered organic molecules that represent the building blocks for life.

Mars “had all the conditions for life to start there when life was starting on Earth,” Andrew Coates, a planetary scientist at University College London’s department of space and climate physics, told the Guardian’s Hannah Devlin at the time of the discovery. “There’s no known reason why it shouldn’t have started on Mars as well.”

Did you know? The many instruments of Curiosity
NASA's Curiosity rover on Mars was built with multiple tools and cameras.
The Mastcam sits at about human height and is designed to take wide panoramic shots of the Mars surface
MAHLI, the Mars Hand Lens Imager, provides close-up views or Martian rocks and dust.
Spectrometers analyze the chemical makeup of substances found on the Martian surface.
REMS, the Rover Enviromental Monitoring Station, is a mobile weather lab that tracks storms and atmospheric conditions on the planet.

Curiosity isn’t the only rover on the Red Planet, however. NASA’s Perseverance also recently made the news after setting a new record for the farthest distance any vehicle has ever driven on the surface of an extraterrestrial world, according to a statement by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory JPL) at the California Institute of Technology.

"Perseverance builds on the 29-year legacy of our past Mars rovers,” Steven Lee, deputy project manager at the JPL, tells Will Dunham in a different Reuters article, “Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and Curiosity—each incorporating prior lessons and improving our ability to drive on another world.”
